newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Canberra diplomats told to hit Hanson, says official.
newsitem.headline: Canberra diplomats told to hit Hanson, says official.

text.p: Australia's foreign service has been ordered to counter race row politician Pauline Hanson at every chance despite Canberra's low-key public stand against the controversial MP, an official said on Wednesday.

The official, at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, said the government was secretly translating speeches and other information discrediting Hanson to be given to foreign governments and media, as well as rebutting her policies.
"We've been told to counter Hanson," said the official, who declined to be named.

Prime Minister John Howard, attacked for failing to act swiftly and firmly enough against Hanson when she sparked a divisive race row last year, this week abandoned a plan to denounce her in a key speech during an official visit to London.
Defending his stand, Howard warned that publicly taking on Hanson would only boost her standing and credibility.
"I mean, every time you talk about it, it gets another run and everybody says 'isn't this ridiculous and outrageous and terrible'," he told reporters in London this week.
"So you're really caught between the devil and the deep blue sea."
But the foreign service has been quietly told to counter Hanson and spread information discrediting her.
"We've had an order from senior levels to run a campaign that counters what Hanson is saying," the official said.
As part of this strategy, a speech by a senior government member linking Hanson to right-wing extremists was translated into Mandarin and given to Chinese authorities.

Government leaders, including Deputy Prime Minister and Trade Minister Tim Fischer, have warned Hanson was undermining Australia's prosperity by jeopardising trade links with the booming Asia-Pacific region.
Hanson says Australia is in danger of being swamped by Asian immigrants, wants all immigration halted, and objects to foreign investment.

After being dumped by Howard's Liberal Party for comments seen as racist during the 1996 election, the small-town fish and chip shop owner was elected to parliament as an independent but has now formed her own far-right party, One Nation.

Leading opinion polls now show One Nation has about 10 percent support, enough to oust the Australian Democrats as the third force in domestic politics if that is maintained to the next election, due by mid-1999.

In the speech translated into Mandarin, government leader Ron Boswell told parliament's upper house, the Senate, last week that Hanson had ties with Australian groups urging violent and racist policies.

Boswell, the Senate chief for the National Party, the junior member of Howard's ruling coalition, said One Nation was linked to the far-right League of Rights, militant gun lobby groups and other extremist factions.
The link was endorsed by the deputy leader of the Labor opposition, former foreign minister Gareth Evans.
"There is no doubt that she is linked with the militant crazy right and they with her," Evans said.
